title: US midterm cycle has run $137M in AI-made political ads — only 27% carried an AI label
subtitle: The Wesleyan Media Project's running tally identifies about 220 AI-assisted ads so far, with Republican sponsors accounting for 81% of them and 88% of the spending. The 2024 cycle total was under $50,000.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Wesleyan Media Project, which has tracked political advertising since 2010, says US campaigns and PACs have now spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced ads in the 2026 midterm cycle — up from under $50,000 across the entire 2024 cycle. The project has identified around 220 individual ads so far. Only about 27% of them carried any AI disclaimer, a number consistent with the roughly 70% unlabeled share reported by the New York Times. Republicans sponsored 81% of the identified ads and 88% of the dollars. One Wisconsin Democratic candidate, Rebecca Cooke, has sent a cease-and-desist letter over AI ads targeting her.

The disclosure gap is where the policy question lives. Twenty-plus US states have passed laws requiring some form of AI disclosure in political advertising, but the Wesleyan numbers suggest enforcement is ineffective at the pace the tools are being used. In 2024 the technical bar for a convincing generated clip was high enough that only a few shops did it. In 2026 any campaign can produce a photoreal 30-second spot in an afternoon with off-the-shelf models. The researchers themselves note the real count is almost certainly higher — their tally depends on being able to detect AI involvement, and the better the models get, the harder detection gets.

The pattern echoes what happened with digital advertising generally after 2010: regulation lagged capability by roughly a cycle, then caught up only after the harm was documented and litigated. The variable this time is pace. Generated video, voice cloning, and agentic ad-buying are landing simultaneously, and the FEC has not completed its rulemaking on AI disclosure. If 2026 ends with less than one-in-three AI ads labeled and no clear federal remedy, 2028 inherits a baseline where the question is not whether campaigns will use generated media but whether anyone can tell them apart from reality.

A note for learners: develop two habits before the next cycle hits. First, learn to reverse-image-search and reverse-audio-search a political ad before you share it — browser extensions and services make this a 10-second check. Second, when you see a persuasive clip, ask who paid for it and what the sponsor is identifiably known for, not just what the clip appears to show. Media literacy against generated content is less about spotting pixel artifacts (that approach is already failing) and more about sourcing. The question that matters is: who benefits if I believe this?
